scenes.narration: Describe people through their task and situation. First-time visitors finding registration before a session is more useful than everyone who likes technology. Include age, nationality or income only when relevant and supported. Do not invent personal details to make a profile feel real.

scenes.title: Separate roles
scenes.visual: Editable user, beneficiary and decision-maker cards.
scenes.narration: The person using a service may not buy it. A visitor might use information while an organiser approves or pays for a service. These roles are hypotheses until checked. Record the user, beneficiary and possible decision-maker separately; do not assume a buyer from a problem report.

scenes.title: Make evidence visible

scenes.narration: Label each statement with its basis: observed, reported, a documented source, or an assumption to investigate. Missing evidence stays unknown. One conversation does not represent a whole market. Keep anonymous role labels and avoid private identifying details.

scenes.narration: Plan a neutral question about a recent experience. Ask what the person tried, what mattered and what happened next. Avoid asking whether they love your future app. Name an ethical way to reach the group, permission needed, and what would make you revise the snapshot.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Describe the people, not an imaginary perfect customer.

children: A
Customer Snapshot
is a provisional description of one group connected to your chosen problem. A
segment
groups people with relevant shared circumstances; you have not yet proven this is a viable market.

Start with the task and context. “First-time visitors finding registration before a session” is more useful than “everyone at events.” Do not invent age, income, nationality, names or preferences. Include demographic details only when relevant and supported.
User
The person who interacts with a proposed service or current process.
Beneficiary
The person or organisation who may gain value.
Buyer / decision-maker
The person who might approve or pay. Keep this unknown if you have no evidence.
Evidence status
Observed, reported, documented, assumed or unknown. Preserve the basis of each claim.
Illustrative example

A visitor may use directions; an organiser might decide about a service. Neither role nor willingness to pay is established by the example. Ask about the current experience before pitching a solution.
Review problem selection
Review affected people

Simulated Coach · no AI connection
Try four scripted guidance modes. The preview reads your current worksheet locally; it does not send information anywhere.

replies.teach: Start with a specific task/context group. Separate user, beneficiary and buyer; label evidence, assumptions and unknowns.
replies.guide: Describe your group, task, current behaviour and roles. Keep a claim-by-claim evidence ledger and plan a voluntary, privacy-conscious recent-experience question.
replies.review: Customer Snapshot check: {missing} required fields still empty. This scripted check counts fields only; it cannot verify your group, evidence, roles or demand.
replies.challenge: Which details are stereotypes? Have you confused user with buyer? What would change your snapshot? Can people decline participation?

sections.heading: Challenge your picture of the customer.

children: More questions to discuss
Have you confused user with buyer? Are you treating one account as representative? Is your group too broad to reach? Can people decline, and can you learn without names or contact details?
Answer all three. You can retry; all three correct are required for local completion.
